title: TurtLES: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Turbulent 3D Neural PDE Surrogates
authors: Jarno Platenburg, Armand Kassaï Koupaï, Paola Cinnella, Patrick Gallinari
abstract: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate computational fluid dynamics, yet progress is limited by the lack of benchmarks capturing realistic, time-dependent turbulent flows. We introduce TurtLES, a 14 TB dataset of 3D turbulent cylinder wakes in the shear-layer transition regime, computed via high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations. The dataset contains 400 trajectories of 400 time steps each, with 3-11 million points per frame, spanning variations in geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack. Unlike existing datasets, TurtLES combines (i) physically realistic turbulence with an active energy cascade driven by vortex stretching, (ii) dense irregular meshes, and (iii) long-horizon temporal dynamics. We benchmark state-of-the-art neural operators on autoregressive rollouts and identify key failure modes, including temporal instability, loss of small-scale energy, and challenges in learning on large irregular domains. TurtLES provides a new benchmark for evaluating surrogate models on 3D turbulent wakes at industrially relevant mesh resolution.

infographic.key_insight: TurtLES tests neural PDE surrogates on realistic 3D turbulent wakes, exposing rollout instability and loss of small-scale energy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The benchmark helps assess whether AI surrogates can reliably accelerate turbulent-flow CFD at industrially relevant mesh resolutions.
method: Generate 3D cylinder wakes using high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations.
Vary geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack on dense irregular meshes.
Benchmark neural operators through autoregressive temporal rollouts.
infographic.evidence_signal: The 14 TB dataset contains 400 trajectories of 400 time steps each, with 3–11 million points per frame; evaluations identify temporal instability, small-scale energy loss, and difficulties with large irregular domains.
infographic.watch_item: The dataset's scale and irregular meshes may make storage, preprocessing, and model training computationally demanding.
infographic.paper_title: TurtLES: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Turbulent 3D Neural PDE Surrogates

title: A Conservative Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes Formulation for Digital Rock Flow Simulation with Embedded Second-Brinkman Effects
authors: Gospel E. Stewart, Hannah P. Menke, David Egya, Jacqueline Mifsud, Julien Maes
abstract: Accurate pore-scale direct numerical simulation (DNS) typically requires boundary-conforming meshes on fully resolved geometries, which is memory-intensive and often becomes impractical when modelling complex rock geometries. In contrast, the Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes (DBS) framework enables simulations to be performed directly on voxelized micro-CT images. However, the commonly used simplified DBS formulation (DBS1) neglects the second Brinkman term (SBT) and the porosity-gradient viscous-diffusion term, leading to errors in flow-field characterisation and permeability prediction. Although it is well established that the SBT is essential for capturing viscous boundary effects, it is often assumed that its inclusion requires separate discretisation. In this work, we show that no separate discretisation of the SBT is necessary: writing the DBS equation in its conservative form and applying a standard central differencing scheme in a finite-volume discretisation naturally retains the full DBS formulation. We refer to this formulation as DBS2, and validate its implementation in the GeoChemFoam framework (our open-source computational fluid dynamics simulator based on OpenFOAM) using three benchmark cases: (i) microchannel flow, (ii) a 2D heterogeneous micromodel, and (iii) a 3D micro-CT image of Bentheimer sandstone. Simulation results show that the DBS2 formulation reproduces the DNS velocity field exactly in the microchannel and matches DNS permeability to within 1.5-3.8% in the micromodel and Bentheimer cases at matched spatial resolution. In contrast, DBS1 systematically overpredicts permeability (14.1 to 37.9% in our cases) under the same discretization. Notably, the conservative treatment of the viscous stress preserves the computational efficiency of DBS1 while achieving DNS-level accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: A conservative Darcy–Brinkman–Stokes formulation (DBS2) naturally retains second-Brinkman effects through standard finite-volume central differencing, without separate discretisation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: DBS2 enables accurate flow and permeability prediction directly on voxelized rock images while preserving DBS1 computational efficiency.
method: Express the full DBS equation in conservative form.
Apply standard central differencing to retain second-Brinkman and porosity-gradient viscous terms.
Implement and validate DBS2 in GeoChemFoam, based on OpenFOAM.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across microchannel, 2D micromodel, and 3D Bentheimer sandstone benchmarks, DBS2 exactly reproduced the microchannel DNS velocity field and matched DNS permeability within 1.5–3.8% in the other cases; DBS1 overpredicted permeability by 14.1–37.9%.
infographic.watch_item: Validation covers three benchmarks at matched spatial resolution; accuracy on other rock geometries and coarser voxel grids remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: A Conservative Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes Formulation for Digital Rock Flow Simulation with Embedded Second-Brinkman Effects

title: Modelling velocity gradient invariants in turbulence with Lundgren spiral vortex ensemble
authors: Zhi Zheng, Weiyu Shen, Jin-Han Xie, Yue Yang
abstract: We investigate the joint probability density function $P(Q,R)$ of invariants $Q$ and $R$ of the velocity gradient tensor in the synthetic turbulent field formed from the Lundgren spiral vortex ensemble, which is referred to as the woven Lundgren turbulence (WLT). The WLT inherently captures non-Gaussian vorticity correlations and multiscale interactions, which are essential for reproducing $P(Q,R)$ observed in homogeneous isotropic turbulence. By analyzing the contributions of stretching, winding and dissipation processes in WLT, we demonstrate that the $Q$-$R$ diagram can be divided into three distinct physical regions: a head region dominated by stretching, a body region dominated by spiral vortex arms, and a tail region dominated by dissipation. We systematically vary three key parameters in WLT, the background strain rate, the cutoff age of spiral vortices and the viscous decay factor, and monitor the evolution of $P(Q,R)$ in different topological regions. It is revealed that increasing the stretching rate broadens the head region, larger cutoff ages enhance the inclination of the body region, and reducing viscous factors extends the tail region, thereby mimicking the effects of strain self-amplification and vortex stretching across scales. Based on WLT statistics, we establish and validate an explicit model of $P(Q,R)$ consisting of the stretching, spiral and dissipation contributions. Thus, the WLT provides a physically interpretable framework for understanding the relation between local geometry and global statistics of turbulence.

infographic.key_insight: A Lundgren spiral vortex ensemble links the head, body and tail of turbulence’s Q–R distribution to stretching, spiral arms and dissipation, respectively.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This physically interpretable framework could support synthetic turbulence generation and assessment of velocity-gradient statistics in turbulence models.
method: Construct woven Lundgren turbulence from a spiral vortex ensemble.
Vary background strain rate, vortex cutoff age and viscous decay factor.
Build an explicit P(Q,R) model combining stretching, spiral and dissipation contributions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Parameter sweeps show that stronger strain broadens the head, older vortex cutoffs increase body inclination and weaker viscous decay extends the tail; the explicit model is validated against WLT statistics.
infographic.watch_item: Validation described in the abstract uses synthetic WLT statistics; applicability to wall-bounded or anisotropic engineering flows remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Modelling velocity gradient invariants in turbulence with Lundgren spiral vortex ensemble

title: Numerical Investigations on Bitumen Liberation from Oil Sands Lump
authors: Mohammadhossein Golchin, Siyu Chen, Payman Esmaeili, Petr Nikrityuk, Xuehua Zhang
abstract: The dynamic liberation and digestion of viscous oil-solid aggregates under turbulent flow is a critical transport phenomenon in multiphase chemical processes, including slurry transport, soil remediation, and industrial extraction. A primary industrial application of this phenomenon is oil sands hydrotransport, where pipelines are widely utilized to simultaneously transport and extract bitumen from lump ore. However, optimizing operating conditions requires a fundamental understanding of the localized hydrodynamic mechanisms governing detachment. To address this, a three-dimensional (3D) Eulerian-Eulerian (E-E) CFD approach coupled with k-omega SST turbulence model has been utilized to investigate bitumen detachment dynamics from complex solid matrices. Six numerical cases were analyzed across lump diameters (D) of 4 and 5 cm and particle Reynolds numbers (Re_p) between 2000 and 4000. The simulation results reveal that bitumen liberation is a shear-driven process, occurring only when the shear stresses exerted by the flow on the lump surface exceed a critical threshold value. The bitumen liberation rate increases with higher Re_p and smaller D, due to enhanced local shear forces and reduced particle shielding. Based on these mechanistic insights, a novel semi-empirical shear-driven model was formulated. The proposed model demonstrates excellent predictive accuracy when validated against experimental liberation data, with an error less than 8.3%. Overall, these findings clarify the fluid-particle interactions governing bitumen detachment and offer a robust, physics-based tool for predicting recovery efficiency in industrial hydrotransport operations.

infographic.key_insight: Bitumen liberation is driven by surface shear exceeding a critical threshold, with faster release at higher particle Reynolds numbers and smaller lump diameters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A shear-based predictive model could guide oil sands hydrotransport operating conditions to improve bitumen recovery.
method: 3D Eulerian–Eulerian CFD with k–ω SST turbulence modeling.
Six cases spanning 4–5 cm lump diameters and particle Reynolds numbers of 2000–4000.
Semi-empirical liberation model based on shear-driven detachment.
infographic.evidence_signal: The proposed model was validated against experimental liberation data, with reported error below 8.3%.
infographic.watch_item: Applicability beyond the studied lump sizes and Reynolds numbers requires further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Numerical Investigations on Bitumen Liberation from Oil Sands Lump

title: Direct numerical simulation of turbulent heat transfer in water with temperature-dependent viscosity and conductivity
authors: Davide Modesti, Alessandro Ceci
abstract: We study turbulent forced convection of liquid water in a plane channel by direct numerical simulation (DNS), with temperature-dependent viscosity and thermal conductivity. The simulations cover wall heating and cooling, mean-to-wall temperature ratios from 0.83 to 1.3, wall temperatures from 277 to 360\,K and wall Prandtl numbers from 2 to 12. Compared with constant-property flow at the same bulk Reynolds number, the friction coefficient changes by $-39\,\%$ to $+32\,\%$, the heat transfer coefficient referred to the wall Prandtl number changes by up to a factor of $2.3$, and empirical correlations deviate from the DNS by up to $26\,\%$. Instantaneous fields and spectra show that the wall friction Reynolds number misrepresents the range of turbulent scales, whereas near-wall streaks of velocity and temperature have a common spacing when scaled with the local viscous length. The density is constant, so the mean velocity and temperature defects in the core follow those of constant-property flow. To predict friction and heat transfer, we map the mean profiles onto those of constant-property flow through integral transformations derived from the mean momentum and energy balances, with empirical corrections of the eddy viscosity and diffusivity calibrated on the DNS. This approach, developed for air, is extended to liquids, whose conductivity is not proportional to the viscosity and whose Prandtl number varies across the channel. The inverse transformations predict friction and heat transfer within $2\,\%$ of the DNS, except at the lowest Reynolds numbers. The same corrections, introduced in the Spalart--Allmaras model, halve its friction error.

infographic.key_insight: Accounting for temperature-dependent water properties through corrected integral profile transformations predicts turbulent friction and heat transfer within 2% of DNS, except at the lowest Reynolds numbers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Property-aware predictions can improve water-channel thermal design where constant-property assumptions and empirical correlations misestimate friction and heat transfer.
method: Run plane-channel DNS of heated and cooled water with temperature-dependent viscosity and conductivity.
Derive mean-profile transformations from momentum and energy balances, calibrating turbulent transport corrections against DNS.
Apply the corrections to the Spalart–Allmaras turbulence model.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across wall temperatures of 277–360 K and wall Prandtl numbers of 2–12, DNS shows friction changes of −39% to +32% versus constant-property flow and empirical-correlation errors up to 26%.
infographic.watch_item: The corrections are DNS-calibrated for constant-density plane-channel flow, and transformation accuracy deteriorates at the lowest Reynolds numbers.
infographic.paper_title: Direct numerical simulation of turbulent heat transfer in water with temperature-dependent viscosity and conductivity

title: Impact of compressiblity approximations on atmospheric gravity wave characteristics
authors: Hrishikesh Sivanandan, Matthew Churchfield, Ben Kravitz, Eliot Quon, Mehtab Khan
abstract: Atmospheric gravity waves are a common phenomenon in the atmosphere and are of critical importance to understanding power generation from wind plants. Common sources of atmospheric gravity waves are stratified flow over topography or wind deceleration ahead of wind farms. Simulations to understand atmospheric boundary layer conditions and wind power generation often solve the Navier-Stokes equations in incompressible Boussinesq form, which allows for density variation as a function of potential temperature only; the purpose of this study is to understand how much that simplification matters. In this work, we evaluate simulated internal gravity wave characteristics by modeling stratified flow over bell-shaped hills using three forms of the governing equations: the linearized incompressible Boussinesq form, the full incompressible Boussinesq form, and the fully compressible form. While all formulations predict qualitatively similar wave structures, the compressible equations predict larger parcel displacements at higher altitudes, higher variations in apparent wavelengths, and more differences in wave angle, particularly at low Froude numbers. These differences can be attributed to compressibility and non-linear effects. The physical implications of differing wave characteristics become especially important in low Froude number regimes. These differences can, in turn, lead to differing predictions of wind farm performance and the characteristics of wind farm-induced gravity waves, underscoring the potential importance of compressibility effects in accurately capturing flow behavior in strongly stratified environments.

infographic.key_insight: Compressibility approximations affect simulated atmospheric gravity waves, with fully compressible equations predicting larger high-altitude parcel displacements and greater wavelength and wave-angle differences, especially at low Froude numbers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These differences could alter wind-farm performance predictions in strongly stratified atmospheric conditions.
method: Simulate stratified flow over bell-shaped hills.
Compare linearized Boussinesq, full incompressible Boussinesq, and fully compressible equations.
Evaluate parcel displacement, apparent wavelength, and wave angle.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulations yield qualitatively similar wave structures across formulations but reveal differences attributed to compressibility and nonlinear effects, particularly at low Froude numbers.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports idealized hill-flow simulations, not direct wind-farm validation or quantified power-prediction errors.
infographic.paper_title: Impact of compressiblity approximations on atmospheric gravity wave characteristics

title: Elastic frontogenesis sets the spectra of smooth elastic turbulence
authors: Marco Edoardo Rosti, Andrea Mazzino
abstract: Most turbulent flows are sustained by inertia, which transfers energy across scales and produces characteristic power-law spectra. Yet dilute polymer solutions also exhibit turbulence when inertia is negligible: in this state, known as elastic turbulence, the velocity field remains spatially smooth while both the velocity and the polymer conformation exhibit robust power-law spectra. How a smooth flow, lacking a hierarchy of eddies, generates such multiscale structure has remained unexplained. Here we show that the missing mechanism is elastic frontogenesis, whereby the flow spontaneously organizes polymer stress into thin sheets that are stretched within their plane and compressed across their thickness, causing their amplitude to grow as they become thinner. Because the fronts are sheet-like structures, this amplification-thinning law uniquely determines the polymer conformation spectrum, while the Stokes response transfers the same geometric scaling to the velocity field, reconciling broadband spectra with spatial smoothness. Being geometric rather than model-specific, elastic frontogenesis provides an organizing principle for viscoelastic flows and the viscoelastic analogue of vortex stretching in inertial turbulence.

infographic.key_insight: Elastic turbulence gains broadband spectra from polymer-stress sheets that amplify as they thin, rather than from a hierarchy of inertial eddies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This geometric mechanism could guide modeling of low-inertia polymer flows where elastic stresses generate complex motion despite spatially smooth velocities.
method: Identify elastic frontogenesis: in-plane stretching and cross-sheet compression concentrate polymer stress.
Relate sheet geometry and amplification during thinning to the polymer conformation spectrum.
Use the Stokes response to connect stress scaling to the velocity spectrum.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports robust power-law spectra in velocity and polymer conformation, but provides no numerical exponents, datasets, or evaluation details.
infographic.watch_item: The proposed model-independent mechanism still requires validation across constitutive models and operating regimes.
infographic.paper_title: Elastic frontogenesis sets the spectra of smooth elastic turbulence

title: Parameterized Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Efficient Simulation of Embedded Microfluidic Chip Cooling
authors: Weiheng Li, Zhiyao Jiang, Bai Song
abstract: Embedded microfluidic cooling is a promising technology for dissipating the intense heat generated by high-performance electronic chips. However, the design and optimization of such coolers impose prohibitive computational costs when using conventional numerical solvers. Here, we present a parameterized physics-informed neural network (PINN) as a deep learning framework for rapidly and accurately predicting the thermohydraulic performance of embedded manifold microchannels. By incorporating four geometric dimensions along with three spatial coordinates as the network inputs, the proposed model enables multiphysics prediction across a continuous design space. Remarkably, our predicted velocity and temperature fields differ from finite-element simulations by relative errors of only 8.1% and 5.6%, respectively, while reducing the computational time and cost by over four orders of magnitude. Key to this framework is a composite strategy combining geometric ansatz embedding, the SOAP optimizer, and a thermal-conductivity-based curriculum learning scheme, which helps overcome the convergence challenges inherent in training PINNs for complex three-dimensional flows. Notably, by leveraging a highly optimized JAX backend, the network achieves convergence on a single consumer-grade GPU in less than four hours. Our approach offers a physics-consistent, real-time surrogate model that can substantially accelerate innovations in advanced microfluidic cooling of future electronics.

infographic.key_insight: A parameterized physics-informed neural network predicts embedded microchannel cooling across a continuous geometric design space, with reported simulation speedups exceeding four orders of magnitude.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The surrogate could accelerate the design and optimization of embedded liquid cooling for high-performance electronic chips.
method: Inputs combine four geometric dimensions with three spatial coordinates to predict thermohydraulic fields.
Training combines geometric ansatz embedding, SOAP optimization, and a thermal-conductivity-based curriculum.
An optimized JAX backend enables convergence in under four hours on a single consumer-grade GPU.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against finite-element simulations, the abstract reports relative errors of 8.1% for velocity fields and 5.6% for temperature fields.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify validation coverage across the design space or reliability beyond the trained geometric range.
infographic.paper_title: Parameterized Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Efficient Simulation of Embedded Microfluidic Chip Cooling

title: Beyond Fourier and Laplace: The Hankel Neural Operator for Learning Solution Operators of Differential Equations
authors: Biswanath Barman, Rajendra K. Ray
abstract: Fourier and Laplace neural operators (FNO, LNO) learn kernel integral operators in a transform domain evaluated on a periodic grid. FNO has no explicit mechanism for boundaries, initial states or transients; LNO adds pole--residue symbols but evaluates them on the discrete Fourier grid with unconstrained poles. FNO's error is large on undamped oscillators and grows under grid refinement. We introduce the Hankel neural operator (HNO), derived from the structure of the solution operator. We prove that the solution operator of a well-posed linear constant-coefficient boundary-value problem on an interval is a Toeplitz operator with a rational kernel plus a finite-rank Hankel-type operator carrying boundary information. Classical results of Kronecker, Nehari and Adamyan--Arov--Krein characterise this kernel class: stable poles, finite Hankel rank and norm bounds independent of the interval length. HNO realises the class in three ways: a non-periodic convolution evaluated by the FFT, with a causal form; a closed-loop Lur'e operator for dynamics without fading memory; and a rational Fourier multiplier that contains FNO as a special case. Trained from data alone, HNO has the lowest mean test error on all nine LNO benchmarks and on the Burgers, Darcy and Navier--Stokes benchmarks of FNO; two of these differences, and the Navier--Stokes comparison with a parameter-matched FNO, are not statistically significant. On the six ODE problems it lowers the better baseline's mean error 2.1--5.2 times, and its Darcy error stays nearly constant from $85^2$ to $421^2$ grids, where FNO's grows eightfold. Ablations support each component. Code and data: \hnorepo{}.

infographic.key_insight: The Hankel Neural Operator (HNO) combines rational-kernel convolution with finite-rank boundary corrections to learn differential-equation solution operators beyond periodic Fourier representations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: HNO offers a promising surrogate for fluid and transport simulations where boundaries, persistent dynamics, and grid refinement challenge Fourier-based models.
method: Decomposes linear constant-coefficient boundary-value solution operators into Toeplitz and finite-rank Hankel-type components.
Implements non-periodic FFT convolution, including a causal form, and closed-loop dynamics without fading memory.
Provides a rational Fourier multiplier formulation containing FNO as a special case.
infographic.evidence_signal: HNO achieved the lowest mean test error across nine LNO benchmarks and three FNO benchmarks; six ODE errors improved 2.1–5.2× over the better baseline, while Darcy error stayed nearly constant from 85² to 421² grids.
infographic.watch_item: The structural theorem covers well-posed linear constant-coefficient problems on an interval, and some reported benchmark improvements were not statistically significant.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Fourier and Laplace: The Hankel Neural Operator for Learning Solution Operators of Differential Equations

title: Kinetic Non-Equilibrium Receptivity Analysis of Hypersonic Flows via a Complex Linearized Unified Gas-Kinetic Scheme
authors: Yue Zhang, Caihong Su, Chao Li, Kun Xu
abstract: In the near-space regime, local rarefaction near the leading-edge shock and wall degrades Navier-Stokes-based stability and receptivity analyses due to velocity slip, temperature jumps, and non-equilibrium transport. The unified gas-kinetic scheme (UGKS) provides a multiscale kinetic description spanning continuum to rarefied regimes. Building on this, a complex linearized UGKS (CLUGKS) is developed: first-order perturbations of the discrete UGKS residual are formulated under a time-harmonic assumption with complex amplitudes, converting disturbance equations into a steady elliptic system solved via pseudo-time marching with LU-SGS acceleration. Consequently, kinetic shock structures, wall slip, temperature jumps, and non-Fourier heat fluxes are inherently captured without hybrid coupling. Three benchmarks verify the framework: a standing acoustic wave at an isothermal wall, a Mach 2 normal shock interacting with an obliquely incident acoustic wave, and freestream acoustic receptivity of a hypersonic blunt wedge. The scheme is applied to argon blunt-wedge flows at equivalent altitudes of 40 km and 50 km. At 40 km, UGKS and Navier-Stokes wall responses agree well in period and phase, while wall slip sustains a weakly positive spatial growth rate in UGKS downstream. At 50 km, intensified rarefaction produces a kinetic temperature precursor and a thickened, merged shock layer; while wall-pressure responses remain close, significant deviations emerge in temperature and heat-flux disturbances. These findings show that while continuum models capture dominant wall-pressure signatures under moderate rarefaction, resolving kinetic non-equilibrium across the shock-particularly its thermal footprint-is essential at higher altitudes.

infographic.key_insight: Kinetic non-equilibrium can strongly alter hypersonic temperature and heat-flux disturbances even when Navier–Stokes predictions of wall pressure remain close.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Resolving rarefaction near shocks and walls can improve high-altitude hypersonic receptivity analysis, especially for thermal-response assessment.
method: Linearize the discrete unified gas-kinetic scheme using complex, time-harmonic perturbations.
Solve the resulting steady disturbance system by pseudo-time marching with LU-SGS acceleration.
Capture shock structure, wall slip, temperature jumps, and non-Fourier heat flux without hybrid coupling.
infographic.evidence_signal: Three benchmarks verify the framework; argon blunt-wedge cases at equivalent altitudes of 40 and 50 km show increasing kinetic effects, with pronounced thermal-disturbance differences at 50 km.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to the reported benchmarks and argon wedge cases; broader gas models and geometries require further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Kinetic Non-Equilibrium Receptivity Analysis of Hypersonic Flows via a Complex Linearized Unified Gas-Kinetic Scheme

title: Efficient high-order Discontinuous Galerkin simulations of multi-species high-enthalpy flows
authors: Beatriz Fagá, Georgii Oblapenko, Yiyang Zhu, Daniel Doehring, Manuel Torrilhon
abstract: Numerical simulation of hypersonic vehicles is an attractive approach to investigate the complex phenomena involved in such technologies. For this, second-order finite volume methods (FVM) are the established method in computational fluid dynamics, with the cost of high dissipation in affordable meshes, thus needing refined ones or adaptive mesh refinements techniques to obtain accurate results. An alternative is to make use of high-order discontinuous Galerkin methods, in particular discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method (DGSEM), once it achieves higher formal order of accuracy on element-local polynomial bases. Therefore the goal of this work is to present the numerical simulations of a two-dimensional scramjet configuration to test and verify the applicability of the DGSEM approach for a complex hypersonic flow where shock-shock interactions occur. Results revealed to be in agreement with reference FVM solvers, thus verifying the code implementation.

infographic.key_insight: High-order discontinuous Galerkin spectral element simulations reproduce reference finite-volume results for a two-dimensional scramjet flow with shock–shock interactions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: DGSEM offers an alternative for hypersonic-flow simulation where affordable second-order finite-volume meshes can introduce excessive numerical dissipation.
method: Apply high-order DGSEM with element-local polynomial bases.
Simulate a two-dimensional scramjet configuration with complex hypersonic flow.
Compare results against reference finite-volume solvers.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports agreement with reference finite-volume results, supporting verification of the code implementation.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative error or runtime comparisons, so accuracy and efficiency advantages remain unquantified.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient high-order Discontinuous Galerkin simulations of multi-species high-enthalpy flows

title: Lift-element-based dynamic network of vortex gust-airfoil interactions
authors: So Yamamoto, Kai Fukami
abstract: We construct a lift-element-based (LE) network for analyzing extreme vortex gust-airfoil interactions. The edge weights quantify the magnitude of changes in local lift elements induced by vorticity perturbations. Network broadcast mode analysis then extracts forcing and response modes that characterize input-output pathways over the evolving network. We consider three-dimensional flows around a NACA 0012 airfoil with a Taylor vortex gust at a Reynolds number of 1000 and compare the LE modes with those of a Biot--Savart (BS) network. The leading BS modes highlight the vortical structures formed through the gust-airfoil interactions, whereas the leading LE modes connect the gust impingement on the airfoil to the shear layer thickened by the gust, which lies on the pressure or suction side depending on the gust condition. Perturbations along the leading BS forcing modes amplify or attenuate the gust-induced lift variation, whereas those along the leading LE forcing modes yield a sustained lift increase or decrease. These input-output mode pairs, representing cause-and-effect relationships within the dynamic network, can guide the selection of actuation locations and timing for manipulating transient aerodynamic loads.

infographic.key_insight: Lift-element network modes link vortex-gust impingement to a thickened airfoil shear layer and identify perturbations that produce sustained lift increases or decreases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These cause-and-effect pathways could guide actuator placement and timing to manage transient aerodynamic loads.
method: Construct a dynamic network weighted by local lift-element changes induced by vorticity perturbations.
Use network broadcast analysis to extract forcing–response mode pairs.
Compare lift-element modes with Biot–Savart network modes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Three-dimensional NACA 0012 flows with a Taylor vortex gust at Reynolds number 1000 show that Biot–Savart-mode perturbations amplify or attenuate gust-induced lift variation, while lift-element-mode perturbations yield sustained lift shifts.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish performance at higher Reynolds numbers or demonstrate a practical closed-loop actuator implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Lift-element-based dynamic network of vortex gust-airfoil interactions

title: Experimental Investigation of Heat Transfer in Axisymmetric Open Cavities at Hypersonic Speeds
authors: T. V. Krishna, J. Cohen, S. K. Karthick, Soumya R. Nanda
abstract: An experimental investigation was conducted to characterize the heat-transfer behavior of an axisymmetric cavity mounted on a cone with a semi-apex angle of $(48^ \circ)$ under Mach 6 freestream conditions in a Ludwieg tunnel. The effects of cavity geometry, represented by the length-to-depth ratio $(L/D = 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0,$ and $6.0)$, rear-wall height-to-depth ratio $(h/D = -0.25, 0,$ and $0.5)$, and Reynolds number ($Re_D = 23000 - 74000$) were systematically investigated. Flow-field characteristics and surface heat-transfer behavior were examined using schlieren and planar laser Rayleigh scattering visualization techniques, together with surface pressure and heat-transfer measurements. The results indicate that increasing the cavity length-to-depth ratio leads to a reduction in the downstream Stanton number $(St_d)$. For the longest cavity $L/D = 6$, however, the downstream Stanton number was found to exceed the upstream value $(St_u)$ indicating enhanced heat transfer in the region downstream of the cavity.

infographic.key_insight: Increasing cavity length-to-depth ratio reduced downstream Stanton number, but at L/D = 6, downstream heat transfer still exceeded the upstream value.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Cavity geometry can influence local thermal loads on hypersonic surfaces and should inform thermal-protection design.
method: Tested axisymmetric cavities on a 48° semi-apex-angle cone at Mach 6 in a Ludwieg tunnel.
Varied L/D from 0.5 to 6.0, h/D from −0.25 to 0.5, and Re_D from 23,000 to 74,000.
Combined schlieren and planar laser Rayleigh scattering with surface pressure and heat-transfer measurements.
infographic.evidence_signal: Measurements across five L/D values showed decreasing downstream Stanton number with increasing cavity length, while St_d remained above St_u at L/D = 6.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no uncertainty estimates or quantitative heat-transfer changes, limiting assessment of design margins.
infographic.paper_title: Experimental Investigation of Heat Transfer in Axisymmetric Open Cavities at Hypersonic Speeds

title: Why fluid relaxation modes matter: Nonlinear frequency response, dynamical integrity, and dynamic pull-in of electrostatic microbeams with squeeze-film damping
authors: Fehmi Najar
abstract: The squeeze film between an electrostatically actuated microbeam can both induce damping and add stiffness to the structure. In addition, the dynamics of the film can interact with the nonlinear response of the microbeam. This paper extends a reduced-order model built on the complex modes of the coupled fluid-structure problem to the computation of periodic responses and their stability for clamped-clamped microbeams. Periodic orbits are continued in the frequency domain, and their stability is determined from their Floquet multipliers. The robustness of the response is assessed through basins of attraction, integrity measures, and dynamic pull-in maps in the plane of the excitation parameters. The model is validated against the measured and computed frequency response of a microswitch. Closed-form expressions are derived for the fluid relaxation modes, together with a correction for strongly coupled films, and define a parameter that characterizes the regime of the film. The approach is applied to different microbeams including cases where fluid modes relax on the timescale of the oscillation. For all simulated devices, a single fluid mode is necessary and sufficient, whereas adding coupled modes cannot replace it, whether the fluid modes respond quasi-statically or carry their own dynamics. Removing the fluid mode displaces both bifurcations that bound the pull-in band, changes the size of the basins of attraction and the position of the attractor within them, misses an abrupt erosion of the safe basin under increasing excitation, and shifts the whole region of dynamic pull-in in the excitation plane. The reduced model, with three real unknowns, makes these global analyses affordable for a fully coupled fluid-structure system.

infographic.key_insight: Retaining one fluid relaxation mode is essential to predict nonlinear response and dynamic pull-in in squeeze-film-damped electrostatic microbeams.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A compact fluid–structure model can help engineers assess operating stability and pull-in risk without neglecting critical squeeze-film dynamics.
method: Build a reduced-order model from coupled fluid–structure complex modes, retaining a fluid relaxation mode.
Continue periodic responses in the frequency domain and assess stability using Floquet multipliers.
Map basins of attraction, dynamical integrity, and dynamic pull-in across excitation parameters.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was validated against measured and computed microswitch frequency responses; one fluid mode was necessary and sufficient for all simulated devices.
infographic.watch_item: The one-fluid-mode finding is demonstrated for the simulated devices and should be checked before extending it to other geometries or operating regimes.
infographic.paper_title: Why fluid relaxation modes matter: Nonlinear frequency response, dynamical integrity, and dynamic pull-in of electrostatic microbeams with squeeze-film damping

title: Variational principles for dissipative continua: transport theorems, inertia, and the minimum-maximum duality
authors: Wolfgang Flachberger, Lukas Einkemmer
abstract: Variational principles for dissipative processes come in two families: minimum principles at nonequilibrium stationary states (Helmholtz, Kirchhoff, Prigogine) and maximum principles for relaxation in continuum mechanics (Ziegler, Hackl, Fischer). We contribute to the understanding of the thermodynamic extremal principle (TEP) by investigating its extremal properties, and uncover the connection between the two families, whose distinction was recently made precise for diffusion: the extremal character is decided by the regime, which is either relaxation at frozen state, as in a closed system (maximum dissipation), or a driven stationary state in an open system (minimum dissipation), while the underlying Rayleighian functional is convex and minimized in both cases. We further examine the Reynolds transport theorem, a useful tool for fixing the energy rates of continua, and the role of inertia, recently argued to lie beyond the reach of Rayleighian principles. With inertia the driving force must be held fixed during the variation, which is less elegant than in the inertialess case, where it is a state function. Writing the energy rate as rates times driving forces still yields the correct equations, and an extremal statement survives whenever the frozen force does not depend on the varied rate. This holds directly for unsteady Stokes flow, and for Navier-Stokes flow after a change to material coordinates, in which the particle acceleration is the second time derivative of the state and the convective term, nonvariational in the Eulerian description, does not appear. The framework is tested on the Navier-Stokes family (Stokes, unsteady Stokes, and Navier-Stokes flow, in order of increasing complexity) and on dissipative Lagrangian mechanics.

infographic.key_insight: Minimum and maximum dissipation principles describe different regimes—driven stationary states and frozen-state relaxation—while the underlying convex Rayleighian is minimized in both.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework clarifies how variational formulations can recover dissipative flow equations, including inertial cases, when forces and coordinate choices are handled consistently.
method: Analyze thermodynamic extremal properties across stationary and relaxation regimes.
Use the Reynolds transport theorem to formulate continuum energy rates.
Hold driving forces fixed during inertial variations and use material coordinates for Navier–Stokes flow.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical tests on Stokes, unsteady Stokes, Navier–Stokes flow, and dissipative Lagrangian mechanics, with no numerical benchmarks or experimental data stated.
infographic.watch_item: With inertia, the extremal statement requires the frozen driving force to be independent of the varied rate; the Eulerian convective term complicates direct variation.
infographic.paper_title: Variational principles for dissipative continua: transport theorems, inertia, and the minimum-maximum duality

title: Parametric spatio-temporal reduced-order modelling via Spectral Proper Orthogonal Decomposition and Gaussian Process Regression
authors: Guglielmo Padula, Antonio Colanera, Gianluigi Rozza
abstract: We present SPOD-GPR, a non-intrusive, parametric, spatio-temporal reduced-order model (ROM) that combines Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD), Spectral POD (SPOD), and Gaussian Process Regression (GPR). A parametric POD first projects the high-dimensional state onto a low-dimensional subspace. The reduced trajectories are then divided into windowed sections, transformed into the frequency domain, and truncated to the most energetic frequencies. SPOD is then performed independently at each retained frequency, yielding temporally coherent modes and coefficients. The parametric dependence of the POD and SPOD bases is modelled by GPR on a local chart of the Grassmann manifold after Procrustes alignment. The SPOD modal coefficients are learned both as explicit functions of the parameters and through a parameter-conditioned autoregressive model that allows for temporal extrapolation beyond the training window. Gaussian processes are sampled jointly and pathwise via Matheron conditioning, ensuring that each predictive realization carries uncertainty quantification consistent with the posterior distribution. The method is tested on four parametric examples where the parameter values and the prediction horizon lie outside the training data: the two-dimensional anisotropic Kuramoto--Sivashinsky equation in a time-periodic and a travelling-wave regime, each parametrised by one of its two coefficients; flow past a cylinder parametrised by the Reynolds number; and flow past an elliptic obstacle parametrised by its semi-axes. In all cases, SPOD-GPR reduces the normalised mean absolute error compared to a POD-GPR baseline, and improves the calibration of the predictive uncertainty, especially in the fluid flow cases, where POD-GPR is severely overconfident. This opens the way to spectral, uncertainty-aware reduced-order models for many-query and real-time applications, such as digital twins.

infographic.key_insight: SPOD-GPR combines spectral reduced-order modelling with Gaussian process regression to improve parametric predictions and uncertainty calibration over a POD-GPR baseline.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support uncertainty-aware flow prediction for many-query engineering tasks and real-time digital twins.
method: Compress states with parametric POD, then window trajectories and retain their most energetic frequencies.
Apply SPOD at each retained frequency and learn parameter-dependent bases using aligned Grassmann-manifold representations and GPR.
Learn modal coefficients with direct and parameter-conditioned autoregressive GPR, using joint pathwise sampling for predictive uncertainty.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two Kuramoto–Sivashinsky regimes, cylinder flow and elliptic-obstacle flow, tests outside the training parameters and time horizon showed lower normalised mean absolute error and better uncertainty calibration than POD-GPR.
infographic.watch_item: Performance beyond the tested extrapolation ranges and computational costs for real-time deployment are not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Parametric spatio-temporal reduced-order modelling via Spectral Proper Orthogonal Decomposition and Gaussian Process Regression

title: Phase-resolved turbulence dynamics in cardiac-cycle-inspired pulsatile pipe flow
authors: Xinyu Wang, Yan Bao, Benlong Wang
abstract: Direct numerical simulations examine the phase-dependent turbulence dynamics of pipe flow driven by cardiac-cycle-inspired waveforms. Four cases with and without a low-flow plateau span two Reynolds-number ranges. The response follows four stages of turbulent--turbulent reorganisation. Strong acceleration suppresses transverse fluctuations and vortical activity. During acceleration and early deceleration, streamwise-normal-stress production recovers ahead of pressure--strain redistribution and radial momentum transport, allowing energy to accumulate in elongated streaks. In early deceleration, near-wall high-speed streaks develop predominantly varicose disturbances associated with Q4 sweeps, whereas outer-buffer-layer low-speed streaks develop predominantly sinuous disturbances associated with Q2 ejections. The transition exhibits distinct radial sequences: Q2-based local onset occurs progressively later towards the wall, whereas Q4-based onset is nearly simultaneous across the viscous sublayer and buffer layer, with peaks occurring successively outwards. The two responses overlap between the drag minimum and recovery maximum as redistribution intensifies markedly and multiscale momentum transport recovers rapidly. Turbulence then decays and its scales readjust. Where present, the plateau prolongs this decay and weakens the turbulence inherited by the next acceleration stage. It further delays local instability and lengthens the onset-to-peak intervals of the shear contributions. An unsteady friction decomposition links these phase-dependent dynamics to the drag response, highlighting the role of delayed turbulent shear recovery in sustaining the low-drag interval.

infographic.key_insight: Cardiac-cycle-inspired pulsation temporarily suppresses turbulence, while delayed turbulent shear recovery sustains a low-drag interval before momentum transport rebounds.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding phase-dependent turbulence recovery could guide pulsatile pipe-flow control strategies that target drag reduction.
method: Direct numerical simulations of cardiac-cycle-inspired pulsatile pipe flow.
Four cases spanning two Reynolds-number ranges, with and without a low-flow plateau.
Phase-resolved turbulence analysis and unsteady friction decomposition.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the simulated cases, streamwise-stress production recovers before redistribution and radial transport, while a low-flow plateau prolongs turbulence decay and delays local instability.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports four simulation cases but no experimental validation, so transfer to broader operating conditions remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Phase-resolved turbulence dynamics in cardiac-cycle-inspired pulsatile pipe flow

title: Bathyspheres, dust devils, lunar plumes and Martian drones: a generalised mathematical model for particle-fluid flow fields generated by static particle bed entrainment across macroscopic scales
authors: S. Langdon, D. J. Needham
abstract: We consider a recently derived mathematical model for the mechanism by which a wind driven flow entrains particles into a fluid from an otherwise static particle bed, a process that is fundamental in initiating and driving the phenomenon of particle cloud formation. This model was previously applied to the "helicopter brownout" problem, in which, as a helicopter descends towards a bed of sand, the downwash and swirling flow from the rotors entrain particles into the air, forming a high-velocity particle-laden cloud around the helicopter. Here, we define a new measure of particle cloud formation potential, outline how the model can be incorporated into existing Computational Fluid Dynamics software, and extend the model to scenarios including: formation of particle clouds in the absence of swirl, such as those caused by a bathysphere descending to the ocean bed, or a rocket landing on the lunar surface, in which case we can precisely predict the critical height above the surface at which particle cloud formation is initiated; generation of dust clouds by less powerful downwash and swirling flows caused by drones or other smaller rotorcraft, such as NASA's Ingenuity Mars helicopter, in which case gravitational effects are included in the model; formation of dust devils (dust clouds formed within and around an upwardly circulating columnar air flow), in which case downwash is replaced by updraft. In each case, predictive models are derived through minor adaptations to key modelling assumptions.

infographic.key_insight: A generalised particle–fluid model predicts how flows entrain particles from static beds across settings ranging from underwater vehicles to lunar landers, Martian drones and dust devils.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could support CFD prediction of particle-cloud onset and formation around vehicles operating near loose sediment or dust.
method: Extend an existing helicopter-brownout entrainment model through targeted changes to modelling assumptions.
Define a measure of particle-cloud formation potential and outline integration into existing CFD software.
Adapt the model for swirl-free flows, gravity-sensitive small rotorcraft and updraft-driven dust devils.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical predictions, including a critical onset height for swirl-free cases, but provides no experimental validation or quantitative accuracy results.
infographic.watch_item: Applicability depends on scenario-specific modelling assumptions; CFD integration is outlined rather than demonstrated in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Bathyspheres, dust devils, lunar plumes and Martian drones: a generalised mathematical model for particle-fluid flow fields generated by static particle bed entrainment across macroscopic scales

title: Some analytical solutions for the evaporative flux and the flow inside a sessile droplet in cylindrical-cap geometry
authors: Lennon Ó Náraigh, Conor Quigley
abstract: We investigate the evaporation of sessile droplets in a two-dimensional (cylindrical-cap) geometry. To circumvent the singularity in the fundamental solution of the Laplace problem for the vapour diffusion in two dimensions, previous works have imposed a far-field boundary condition at an arbitrary distance from the droplet. To remove this arbitrary distance, we extend the approach of Yariv [Physical Review E, 107(6), p. L063101, 2023] for slender droplets (zero contact angles) to droplets with arbitrary contact angles. Using conformal mapping, we obtain an explicit expression for the evaporative flux for arbitrary contact angles, and verify the result via numerical simulation. We couple the evaporative flux to the Stokes flow inside the droplet and use a local analysis to characterize the flow near the triple point. For contact angles below $90^\circ$, the evaporative flux exhibits the same power-law divergence in the two-dimensional geometry as in the corresponding three-dimensional (spherical-cap) geometry. The flow near the triple point likewise has the same power-law dependence in the two geometries. Our expressions for the evaporative flux and flow inside the droplet are explicit and involve no special functions, and therefore provide a simple explanation of the mechanism which drives the contact-line flow in evaporating sessile droplets.

infographic.key_insight: Explicit analytical solutions describe evaporation and near-contact-line flow in cylindrical-cap droplets, with the same local power-law behavior as spherical-cap droplets for contact angles below 90°.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These solutions offer simple benchmarks for modeling evaporation-driven contact-line transport in two-dimensional droplet geometries.
method: Extend a slender-droplet approach to arbitrary contact angles without an arbitrary far-field distance.
Use conformal mapping to derive explicit evaporative-flux expressions.
Couple evaporation to internal Stokes flow and analyze the triple-point region.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical verification of the analytical evaporative flux but provides no quantitative error metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The model assumes cylindrical-cap geometry and Stokes flow; matching local exponents does not establish full equivalence with three-dimensional droplets.
infographic.paper_title: Some analytical solutions for the evaporative flux and the flow inside a sessile droplet in cylindrical-cap geometry

title: Purely elastic centre-mode instability in channel and pipe flows of a simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner fluid
authors: Calum S. Skene, Jeffrey S. Oishi, Keaton J. Burns, Moritz Linkmann, Geoffrey M. Vasil, Alexander Morozov
abstract: Recent work identified spatially localised midplane stress structures as the building blocks of chaotic behaviour in pressure-driven parallel shear flows of viscoelastic fluids. Such coherent structures are thought to originate from a linear centre-mode instability of the laminar state. In the absence of inertia, however, the Oldroyd-B and FENE-P constitutive models predict that this instability is confined to ultra-dilute polymer solutions and very large Weissenberg numbers in channel flow, while no purely elastic instability has been reported in pipe flow. Here, we study numerically the linear stability of channel and pipe flows of a simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner (sPTT) fluid and find a purely elastic centre-mode instability in both geometries across a wide range of polymer concentrations and at much lower Weissenberg numbers. Since the sPTT and FENE-P models have identical steady rheology and laminar profiles, their contrasting predictions indicate that the existence of the centre-mode instability is governed by the transient rheological response of the fluid. Our results suggest that the purely elastic centre-mode instability should be observable under realistic flow conditions. They also offer a means of discriminating between constitutive models.

infographic.key_insight: A simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner (sPTT) fluid exhibits a purely elastic centre-mode instability in both channel and pipe flows, implicating transient rheology rather than steady flow properties.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The findings suggest that inertia-free instabilities may arise under realistic viscoelastic flow conditions and help distinguish constitutive models for engineering simulations.
method: Numerically analyse linear stability of pressure-driven sPTT channel and pipe flows.
Identify centre-mode instability in the absence of inertia.
Compare predictions with Oldroyd-B and FENE-P models.
infographic.evidence_signal: The numerical study finds instability across a wide range of polymer concentrations and at much lower Weissenberg numbers than previously predicted, despite sPTT and FENE-P sharing identical steady rheology and laminar profiles.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports linear numerical predictions, not experimental confirmation or proof that the instability develops into sustained chaotic flow.
infographic.paper_title: Purely elastic centre-mode instability in channel and pipe flows of a simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner fluid
